questions.problem:
$$
{x}^{′}=[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]x,\,{x}_{1}(t)=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t},\,{x}_{2}(t)=[\begin{aligned}2t \\ -1\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t}
$$

Consider the system of linear ODEs and two of its linearly independent solutions ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2},$ shown above. Which of the following is a fundamental matrix for the system?
questions.worked_solution:
Given a linear system ${x}^{′}=Ax,$ where $A$ is an $n\times n$ matrix, a *fundamental matrix* $Φ(t)$ of the system is an $n\times n$ matrix whose columns are linearly independent solutions of the system.

In our case, we have a $2\times 2$ system. We are also given that the two linearly independent solutions of the system are the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t}=[\begin{aligned}2{e}^{3t} \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ {x}_{2}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}2t \\ -1\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t}=[\begin{aligned}2t{e}^{3t} \\ -{e}^{3t}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, our fundamental could be written as

$$
Φ(t)=[\begin{aligned}2{e}^{3t} & 2t{e}^{3t} \\ 0 & -{e}^{3t}\end{aligned}].
$$

**Note:** The columns of $Φ$ can be written in any order.

questions.problem:
Consider the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant $2\times 2$ matrix. Let $Φ(t)$ be a fundamental matrix for this system. A derivation showing that $Φ(t)$ satisfies the matrix differential equation ${Φ}^{′}(t)=A\,Φ(t)$ is given below.

*Hint: $[a,\,b]$ denotes a matrix whose columns are vectors $a$ and $b.$*

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let $Φ(t)=[{x}_{1}(t),\,{x}_{2}(t)]$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{1}^{′}(t)=A{x}_{1}(t)$

$\text{L3}:\,$ ${x}_{2}^{′}(t)=A{x}_{2}(t)$

$\text{L4}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}(t)=[{x}_{1}^{′}(t),\,{x}_{2}^{′}(t)]$

$\text{L5}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}(t)=[A{x}_{1}(t),\,A{x}_{2}(t)]$

$\text{L6}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}(t)=A[{x}_{1}(t),\,{x}_{2}(t)]$

$\text{L7}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}(t)=AΦ(t)$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L3}$ follows from the fact that $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix and line $\text{L1}$ by the {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L4}$ follows from line $\text{L1}$ by {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L6}$ follows from line $\text{L5}$ by {{field-3}}.
questions.worked_solution:
Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L3}.$ Since $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns are solutions of the homogeneous system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t).$ Line $\text{L1}$ identifies ${x}_{2}(t)$ as a column of $Φ(t),$ so ${x}_{2}(t)$ must satisfy the differential equation. In particular,

$$
{x}_{2}^{′}(t)=A{x}_{2}(t).
$$

Therefore, $\text{L3}$ follows from the fact that $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix and line $\text{L1}$ by the $\text{definition of a fundamental matrix}.$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L4}.$ Since $Φ(t)=[{x}_{1}(t),\,{x}_{2}(t)],$ the derivative of $Φ(t)$ is obtained by differentiating each column:

$$
{Φ}^{′}(t)=[{x}_{1}^{′}(t),\,{x}_{2}^{′}(t)].
$$

Thus, $\text{L4}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by $\text{differentiating each column}.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L5}$ and $\text{L6}.$ We now factor the matrix $A$ on the left:

$$
{Φ}^{′}(t)=[A{x}_{1}(t),\,A{x}_{2}(t)]=A[{x}_{1}(t),\,{x}_{2}(t)].
$$

Therefore, $\text{L6}$ follows from $\text{L5}$ by $\text{factoring out }A\text{ on the left}.$

questions.problem:
Consider the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant $2\times 2$ matrix. Let $Φ(t)$ be a fundamental matrix for this system. A derivation showing that every solution $x(t)$ can be written in the form $x(t)=Φ(t)\,c$ for some constant vector $c=[{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}]^{T}$ is given below.

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ be the columns of $Φ(t)$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ form a basis of solutions

$\text{L3}:\,$ $x(t)$ can be written as $x(t)={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t)$

$\text{L4}:\,$ $Φ(t)\,c={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t)$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $x(t)=Φ(t)\,c$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L2}$ follows from {{field-1}} by the definition of a fundamental matrix.

$\,$ Line $\text{L4}$ follows from line $\text{L1}$ by the {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L5}$ follows from lines {{field-3}} by {{field-4}}.
questions.worked_solution:
Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}.$ Since $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ form a basis of the solution space for our system. Thus, $\text{L2}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by the definition of a fundamental matrix.

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L4}.$ Since ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ are the columns of $Φ(t),$ we can write

$$
Φ(t)=[\begin{aligned}\,| & | \\ {x}_{1}(t) & {x}_{2}(t) \\ \,| & |\end{aligned}].
$$

Then by the definition of matrix multiplication,

$$
Φ(t)\,c=[\begin{aligned}\,| & | \\ {x}_{1}(t) & {x}_{2}(t) \\ \,| & |\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{aligned}]={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t).
$$

Thus, $\text{L4}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by the $\text{definition of matrix multiplication}.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L3}$ and $\text{L4}.$ In $\text{L3}$ we have $x(t)={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t),$ and in $\text{L4}$ we have $Φ(t)c={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t).$ Since both expressions are equal to the same quantity, the transitive property of equality gives $x(t)=Φ(t)c.$ Thus, $\text{L5}$ follows from $\text{L3 and L4}$ by the $\text{the transitive property of equality}.$

questions.problem:
Consider the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant $2\times 2$ matrix. Let $Φ(t)$ be a fundamental matrix for this system. A derivation showing that $Φ(t)$ is invertible for all $t$ is given below.

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ be the columns of $Φ(t)$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ are linearly independent for all $t$

$\text{L3}:\,$ $det(Φ(t))\ne 0$ for all $t$

$\text{L4}:\,$ $Φ(t)$ is invertible for all $t$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L2}$ states the independence of the columns of {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L2}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by the {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L4}$ follows from line $\text{L3}$ by the {{field-3}}.
questions.worked_solution:
Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first interpret line $\text{L2}.$ Line $\text{L2}$ states that the two columns of $Φ(t)$ are linearly independent, which is required of a fundamental matrix. Thus, $\text{L2}$ states independence of the columns of $Φ(t).$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}.$ Since $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ form a basis of the solution space for our system. Thus, $\text{L2}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by the $\text{definition of a fundamental matrix}.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L3}$ and $\text{L4}.$ Recall that a square matrix is invertible when its determinant is nonzero. Since in $\text{L3}$ we have that $det(Φ(t))\ne 0$ for all $t,$ it follows that $Φ(t)$ is invertible for all $t.$ Thus, $\text{L4}$ follows from $\text{L3}$ by the $\text{properties of invertible matrices}.$

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 5 \\ -5 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the system of linear ODEs ${x}^{′}=Ax$ with the matrix $A$ shown above. Compute the **standard** fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ for this system.

| ${Φ}_{0}(t)=\,\,$ |  | {{field-1}} | {{field-2}} |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | {{field-3}} | {{field-4}} |  |  |
questions.worked_solution:
Suppose $A$ is a constant $n\times n$ matrix and $x(t)$ is an $n\times 1$ column vector. The standard fundamental matrix of the linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ denoted ${Φ}_{0}(t),$ is the unique matrix solution of the initial value problem 

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n},
$$

where ${I}_{n}$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}[\begin{aligned}0 & 5 \\ -5 & 0\end{aligned}]t+{\alpha }_{0}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} & 5{\alpha }_{1}t \\ -5{\alpha }_{1}t & {\alpha }_{0}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=5\text{i}t,\,{\lambda }_{2}=-5\text{i}t,
$$

which are complex conjugates. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}r((5\text{i})t) & ={e}^{(5\text{i})t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}(5\text{i})t+{\alpha }_{0} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t) \\ {\alpha }_{0}+5\text{i}{\alpha }_{1}t & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we equate the real and imaginary parts, and solve for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t) \\ 5{\alpha }_{1}t=\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}\,⇒\,{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t) \\ {\alpha }_{1}=\frac{1}{5t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t) \\ 5{\alpha }_{1}t & =5\cdot \frac{1}{5t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)\cdot t \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(5t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}].
$$

\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}]t+{\alpha }_{0}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} & 2{\alpha }_{1}t \\ 2{\alpha }_{1}t & {\alpha }_{0}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=-2t,\,{\lambda }_{2}=2t,
$$

both of multiplicity one. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}r(-2t)={e}^{-2t} \\ r(2t)={e}^{2t}\end{aligned}\,⇒\,{\begin{aligned}-2t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-2t} \\ 2t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{2t}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- Subtraction the second equation from the first one, we get

$$
-4t{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{-2t}-{e}^{2t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{1}=-\frac{1}{4t}({e}^{-2t}-{e}^{2t}).
$$

- Adding the first and the second equations, we get

$$
2{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-2t}+{e}^{2t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}=\frac{1}{2}({e}^{-2t}+{e}^{2t}).
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{-2t}+{e}^{2t}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{2t}+{e}^{-2t}) \\ 2{\alpha }_{1}t & =2\cdot (-\frac{1}{4t}({e}^{-4t}-{e}^{4t}))t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{2t}-{e}^{-2t})\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t}+{e}^{-2t} & {e}^{2t}-{e}^{-2t} \\ {e}^{2t}-{e}^{-2t} & {e}^{2t}+{e}^{-2t}\end{aligned}].
$$

$$

Consider the system of linear ODEs ${x}^{′}=Ax$ with the matrix $A$ shown above. Compute the **standard** fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ for this system.

| ${Φ}_{0}(t)=\,\,$ |  | {{field-1}} | {{field-2}} |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | {{field-3}} | {{field-4}} |  |  |
questions.worked_solution:
Suppose $A$ is a constant $n\times n$ matrix and $x(t)$ is an $n\times 1$ column vector. The standard fundamental matrix of the linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ denoted ${Φ}_{0}(t),$ is the unique matrix solution of the initial value problem 

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n},
$$

where ${I}_{n}$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}[\begin{aligned}5 & 1 \\ 0 & 5\end{aligned}]t+{\alpha }_{0}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & {\alpha }_{1}t \\ 0 & 5{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The only eigenvalue of $At$ is 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=5t
$$

of multiplicity two. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}r(5t)={e}^{5t} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\lambda }r(5t)={e}^{5t}\end{aligned}\,⇒\,{\begin{aligned}5t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{5t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}={e}^{5t}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- From the second equation, we get

$$
{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{5t}.
$$

- Substituting this into the first one, we get

$$
5t{e}^{5t}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{5t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{5t}(1-5t).
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}5{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =5{e}^{5t}t+{e}^{5t}(1-5t) \\  & ={e}^{5t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}t & ={e}^{5t}t \\  & =t{e}^{5t}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{5t} & t{e}^{5t} \\ 0 & {e}^{5t}\end{aligned}].
$$

questions.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ -2 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the system of linear ODEs ${x}^{′}=Ax$ with the matrix $A$ shown above. Compute the **standard** fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ for this system.

| ${Φ}_{0}(t)=\,\,$ |  | {{field-1}} | {{field-2}} |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | {{field-3}} | {{field-4}} |  |  |
questions.worked_solution:
Suppose $A$ is a constant $n\times n$ matrix and $x(t)$ is an $n\times 1$ column vector. The standard fundamental matrix of the linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ denoted ${Φ}_{0}(t),$ is the unique matrix solution of the initial value problem 

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n},
$$

where ${I}_{n}$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ -2 & 0\end{aligned}]t+{\alpha }_{0}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} & 2{\alpha }_{1}t \\ -2{\alpha }_{1}t & {\alpha }_{0}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=2\text{i}t,\,{\lambda }_{2}=-2\text{i}t,
$$

which are complex conjugates. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}r((2\text{i})t) & ={e}^{(2\text{i})t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}(2\text{i})t+{\alpha }_{0} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ {\alpha }_{0}+2\text{i}{\alpha }_{1}t & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we equate the real and imaginary parts, and solve for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) \\ 2{\alpha }_{1}t=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}\,⇒\,{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) \\ {\alpha }_{1}=\frac{1}{2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) \\ 2{\alpha }_{1}t & =2\cdot \frac{1}{2t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\cdot t \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}].
$$

Consider the system of linear ODEs and two of its linearly independent solutions $\mathbf x_1$ and $\mathbf x_2,$ shown above. Find the fundamental matrix for the system.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Given a linear system $\mathbf{x}' = A \mathbf{x},$ where $A$ is an $n \times n$ matrix, a *fundamental matrix* $\Phi(t)$ of the system is an $n \times n$ matrix whose columns are linearly independent solutions of the system.

In our cases, we have a $2 \times 2$ system. We are also given that the two linearly independent solutions of the system are the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{5t}=[\begin{aligned}4{e}^{5t} \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ {x}_{2}(t) & =[\begin{aligned}4t \\ 4\end{aligned}]{e}^{5t}=[\begin{aligned}4t{e}^{5t} \\ 4{e}^{5t}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, our fundamental could be written as
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14070844/assets/bb710709a593f8d185cde601fb5082d7f79ed21af824c28949477d2011479d95.png)

**Note:** The columns of $\Phi$ can be written in any order.

canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the system $\mathbf{x}'(t) = A \mathbf{x}(t),$ where $A$ is a constant $2 \times 2$ matrix. Let $\Phi(t)$ be a fundamental matrix for this system. A derivation showing that $\Phi(t)$ satisfies the matrix differential equation $\Phi'(t) = A \, \Phi(t)$ is given below.

*Hint: $\big[ \mathbf{a}, \: \mathbf{b} \big]$ denotes a matrix whose columns are vectors $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}.$*

$\textrm{L1}{:}\;$ Let $\Phi(t) = \big[ \mathbf{x}_1(t), \: \mathbf{x}_2(t) \big]$

$\textrm{L2}{:}\;$ $\mathbf{x}_1'(t) = A \mathbf{x}_1(t)$

$\textrm{L3}{:}\;$ $\mathbf{x}_2'(t) = A \mathbf{x}_2(t)$

$\textrm{L4}{:}\;$ $\Phi'(t) = \big[ \mathbf{x}_1'(t), \: \mathbf{x}_2'(t) \big]$

$\textrm{L5}{:}\;$ $\Phi'(t) =  \big[ A \mathbf{x}_1(t), \: A \mathbf{x}_2(t) \big]$

$\textrm{L6}{:}\;$ $\Phi'(t) = A \big[ \mathbf{x}_1(t), \: \mathbf{x}_2(t) \big]$

$\textrm{L7}{:}\;$ $\Phi'(t) = A \Phi(t)$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\quad$ Line $\textrm{L2}$ follows from the fact that ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14070844/assets/be39ec10432eb81c3e00fdf30599353450e1ae7ebebd136f20dce45deb685cac.png).

$\quad$ Line $\textrm{L6}$ follows from line $\textrm{L5}$ by ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14070844/assets/09febb48bb00d22caebf088103181b5db6377befccad18f1370718351cc91e9d.png).

$\quad$ Line $\textrm{L7}$ follows from line $\textrm{L6}$ and substitution from line ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14070844/assets/999db06dcfe0878ddb3316b11546668ba9442d8fd110165e5076b90964b84905.png).
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first consider line $\textrm{L2}.$ Since $\Phi(t)$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns $\mathbf{x}_1(t)$ and $\mathbf{x}_2(t)$ are linearly independent solutions of the homogeneous system $\mathbf{x}'(t) = A \mathbf{x}(t).$ This means that each column satisfies the differential equation. In particular,

$$
\mathbf{x}_1'(t) = A \mathbf{x}_1(t).
$$

Therefore, $\textrm{L2}$ follows from the fact that $\mathbf{x}_1$ is a solution of the system.

- Next, we consider lines $\textrm{L5}$ and $\textrm{L6}.$ We now factor the matrix $A$ on the left:

$$
\Phi'(t)=\big[A\mathbf{x}_1(t),\:A\mathbf{x}_2(t)\big]
= A\big[\mathbf{x}_1(t),\:\mathbf{x}_2(t)\big].
$$

Therefore, $\textrm{L6}$ follows from $\textrm{L5}$ by factoring out $A$ on the left.

- Finally, we consider lines $\textrm{L6}$ and $\textrm{L7}.$ From $\textrm{L6}$ we have $\Phi'(t)=A\big[\mathbf{x}_1(t),\:\mathbf{x}_2(t)\big].$ Using $\Phi(t)=\big[\mathbf{x}_1(t),\:\mathbf{x}_2(t)\big]$ from $\textrm{L1},$ we substitute to obtain $\Phi'(t)=A\Phi(t).$ Thus, $\textrm{L7}$ follows from $\textrm{L6}$ by substitution from $L1.$
